I think it is a good thing, but it's been abused, like everything else.

If you want to get funding from a company to make a game, you have to prove it'll be commercially successful, that there's demand for it. It's considered first and foremost as a product, and not something for fun. You have to tone down or censor certain things because if you rock the boat you probably won't get any money. Investors are often very reluctant to risk their money on something that could prove controversial.

On the other hand, with crowdfunding, you can make things because you're passionate about them. If you can make others believe in you, and your project, then you can make what you want. That's a good thing to be able to do. No constraints (in theory) over what you can put in it, so long as it's legal, potentially much better communication with your backers, often having the chance to make things that a re generally less popular now such as board games that you would have much more trouble securing funding for traditionally.

The problem is, there are people who use this as an excuse to take people's money without doing much work. And then they crak out a garbage product that's little or nothing like what they promised, and vanish off the face of the earth. Or certain people using Patreon to fund themselves, while they fail to deliver on what they said they would in time or quality. And then they have the nerve to criticise people when they complain that they've been ripped off, or accuse them of being entitled or privileged, or some such bullshit to deflect from the truth that they haven't done what they said they would.

At the end of the day, crowdfunding is really what people choose to make of it. You can make a game you would never have had the money for otherwise, or starts a web series where you actually have the money and time to work on it properly..or you can take people's money and vanish, damaging the reputation of yourself and everyone using crowdfunding. It's up to the people using it to make of it what they will. I just hope they don't fuck it up for people who want to use it in the future.

I think it's a good thing that a lot of people try to abuse. Some companies use it to gather money to help build their goods the right way, others take the money and run. Crowdfunding is entirely voluntary. Nobody is wheedling you into reading their literature, while their foot is stuck in your door.

As a youtuber, I've considered it quite a bit. I think that it's a more sustainable model for financing content creation, to be honest. Youtube has been dropping payouts for youtubers lower and lower. It used to be that someone with 100k subs could easily be a full-time youtuber. Now you're lucky if you can do it with less than 300k if you don't have another channel of income like Patreon.
I personally see it as a good thing. It allows the creator to make what he wants without having to worry about making profit.

I like backing projects that interest me, but I wish the crowdfunding companies would do more to vet/govern projects. While it may not work in all cases, I would love to see the project offer up a project plan with milestones that control funding release gates. So like "Upon campaign completion, project receives 20% of funding for to accomplish X (prototyping, hiring, storyboarding, etc), when X is delivered, the project receives 60% of funding to go into production, when production is complete, project recieves 20% to cover delivery."

The company running the site could hold the funds in escrow (and collect some interest to fund themselves/) and standards could be set such as "If target Y is missed by more than N, the project is declared defunct and undispersed funds will be returned to the supporters."
